Authorities have warned that the reduction could strain the system if demand peaks, but have also indicated contingency plans are in place to mitigate disruptions. The action underscores ongoing tensions between labor groups and government officials over cost‑saving measures in the energy sector.
author: France 24

title: EU enforcement gaps allow PFAS in consumer products above legal limits
content:
Eve Irvine announced the appointment of Hélène Duguy, a senior environmental lawyer with ClientEarth, to lead the organization’s efforts on PFAS contamination. The move comes amid growing concern over the prevalence of per‑ and polyfluoroalkyl substances, which have been identified in water, soil, food, consumer goods and even in human tissue across multiple regions.

Duguy highlighted that while scientific understanding of PFAS hazards is extensive, viable alternatives exist for many applications and a comprehensive regulatory framework has already been established. She argued that the principal obstacle is not a lack of knowledge or legislation but the weak enforcement of existing rules, the slow pace of regulatory updates and persistent corporate resistance, which together allow hazardous chemicals to remain in circulation despite existing restrictions. Strengthening compliance mechanisms and accelerating policy implementation are now being positioned as the next critical steps to curb PFAS exposure.
author: France 24

title: Andrew Weissmann claims corruption was endemic in Trump administration
content:
François Picard recently introduced Andrew Weissmann, a professor at NYU School of Law, former general counsel of the FBI and author of the forthcoming book *Liar’s Kingdom*, at a forum focused on governmental accountability. Weissmann highlighted a growing trend in which political deception and deliberate falsehoods are increasingly normalized and employed for strategic advantage, arguing that this dynamic undermines public confidence in both government and its institutions.

Drawing on the arguments presented in *Liar’s Kingdom*, Weissmann questioned the disparity between the legal treatment of political leaders and ordinary citizens, noting that while elected officials often evade accountability for false statements, private individuals can face serious legal repercussions for the same conduct. He called for a reassessment of legal standards to ensure consistent application of the law regardless of political status, emphasizing the need to restore trust in democratic processes.
author: France 24

title: Historian links French political fragmentation to strong National Rally poll numbers
content:
Carys Garland welcomed Dr. Andrew Smith, a historian of modern France and lecturer in liberal arts at Queen Mary University of London, to discuss the latest French presidential polling. Dr. Smith cautioned that the National Rally’s strong showing under Marine Le Pen should not be interpreted as a foregone far‑right victory. He noted that the party’s success is bolstered by voter familiarity, a unified front and a tightly focused message, rather than an inevitable shift in political allegiance.

According to Smith, the poll results reflect a broader mood among French voters marked by anger, anxiety, economic insecurity and political fatigue. He argued that describing the current environment as “polarization” oversimplifies the situation; instead, he proposes the term “fragmentation” to capture the electorate’s divided and unsettled state. The analysis suggests that the National Rally’s appeal is symptomatic of deeper societal stresses rather than a singular ideological surge.
author: France 24

title: Dangote seeks $1.6 billion IPO to fund $14.3 billion refinery expansion
content:
Aliko Dangote’s conglomerate is seeking $1.6 billion in capital from investors to fund a $14.3 billion expansion that would double the capacity of its Lagos‑based oil refinery, the largest single‑site facility in sub‑Saharan Africa. The project, slated to raise the plant’s output from roughly 650,000 to 1.2 million barrels per day, is being financed through a mix of private placement and a potential public offering that could allow individual Nigerians to purchase shares. The company has outlined a timeline that targets completion of the first phase by 2028, with the additional capacity intended to reduce the nation’s reliance on imported refined products and to boost export potential.

Regulatory filings indicate that the offering will be open to qualified institutional investors and, subject to approval by the Nigerian Securities and Exchange Commission, to retail investors meeting specific financial criteria. Analysts note that the minimum subscription amount, set at several hundred thousand naira, may limit participation to higher‑income individuals and corporate entities, raising questions about the extent to which “millions of Nigerians” can realistically acquire a stake. The success of the capital raise will hinge on investor confidence in the refinery’s projected cash flows, the broader economic environment, and the company’s ability to meet the stipulated eligibility thresholds.
author: DW World

title: EU drafts Arctic strategy amid rising geopolitical competition
content:
European policymakers are elevating the Arctic to a priority on the continent’s strategic agenda, driven by a convergence of geopolitical and economic pressures. Heightened Russian military activity in the region, combined with former U.S. President Donald Trump’s public statements threatening U.S. interests in Greenland, have intensified security concerns among European capitals. At the same time, the growing demand for critical raw materials—such as rare earth elements, lithium, and cobalt—has turned the Arctic’s untapped mineral deposits into a focal point for competition among global powers.

In response, the European Union is coordinating a series of initiatives aimed at strengthening its presence and influence in the High North. These include bolstering NATO’s northern flank, investing in sustainable extraction technologies, and negotiating joint research programs with Arctic states to secure supply chains while adhering to environmental standards. By aligning defense, energy, and trade policies, Europe seeks to mitigate external threats, ensure access to essential resources, and maintain a balanced role in the rapidly evolving Arctic landscape.
author: DW World

title: European Space Agency launches two climate observation satellites
content:
The European Space Agency (ESA) has successfully placed two new satellites into low‑Earth orbit, expanding its portfolio of climate‑monitoring assets. Launched aboard a Vega‑C rocket from the Guiana Space Centre, the twin spacecraft are designed to deliver high‑resolution data on the planet’s changing environment, reinforcing ESA’s long‑term commitment to Earth observation and supporting international efforts to track the effects of global warming.

One of the satellites, equipped with a multispectral imaging payload, will concentrate on terrestrial vegetation, measuring parameters such as leaf area index, chlorophyll concentration and phenological cycles to assess how plant ecosystems respond to temperature shifts, drought and other stressors. The companion satellite carries a suite of atmospheric sensors that will monitor greenhouse‑gas concentrations, aerosol levels and sea‑surface temperature. Together, the missions aim to provide near‑real‑time datasets that can improve climate models, inform policy decisions and aid scientists in evaluating mitigation strategies. The ESA expects the satellites to become fully operational within six months, delivering a continuous stream of observations that will enhance understanding of climate dynamics for years to come.
author: DW World

title: Objects found on Dutch railway lines cause major service outage
content:
A significant disruption has struck parts of the Dutch railway network after unidentified objects were discovered on several tracks, prompting an immediate suspension of services. ProRail, the state-owned entity responsible for rail infrastructure, confirmed that the objects were placed deliberately and that the incident appears to be a case of intentional wrongdoing. Emergency crews were dispatched to clear the lines, and train operators halted operations in the affected zones as a safety precaution.

Authorities are investigating the incident while working to restore normal traffic. Preliminary assessments suggest that the objects could have caused severe damage or accidents if trains had continued to run, prompting a swift response from both railway officials and police. Service reductions are expected to continue until the tracks are fully inspected and cleared, and commuters have been advised to seek alternative transport options. The investigation remains ongoing, with officials emphasizing the priority of passenger safety and the restoration of regular service.
author: DW World

title: Saudi coalition pledges firm response to Houthi air strikes
content:
The Saudi-led coalition announced it will respond “firmly” to recent Houthi missile and drone strikes that targeted urban centers within Saudi Arabia, including the capital Riyadh and the coastal city of Jeddah. The attacks, which occurred over the past 48 hours, damaged civilian infrastructure and resulted in several injuries, prompting the coalition’s top commander to issue a statement affirming that any aggression against Saudi territory will be met with decisive military action. The Houthi movement, backed by Iran, has intensified its campaign against Saudi interests since the escalation of the Yemen conflict in 2015, citing retaliation for Saudi airstrikes on Houthi‑controlled areas.

In response, coalition forces have mobilized additional air defense assets and prepared retaliatory strikes against Houthi positions in northern Yemen, aiming to neutralize launch sites and command structures. The coalition’s pledge underscores its commitment to safeguarding Saudi sovereignty while warning that further attacks on civilian areas will trigger escalated operations. International observers noted the heightened risk of broader regional instability, urging restraint from all parties to prevent further civilian casualties.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Mitch McConnell returns to Senate after three-month absence
content:
Senator Mitch McConnell, the Republican leader of the U.S. Senate, cast his first vote since June during a procedural motion on the Senate floor on Tuesday, signaling his return to full participation as the chamber approaches a series of high‑stakes legislative actions. The vote, which approved a motion to bring a budget reconciliation package to the floor, marked McConnell’s first recorded vote after a prolonged absence due to health concerns that kept him away from the chamber for more than three months.

McConnell’s renewed presence comes as Senate leaders prepare to address several critical issues, including the federal debt ceiling, funding for the Department of Defense, and a bipartisan infrastructure bill that require a quorum and decisive votes. By rejoining the roll call, McConnell underscored his commitment to guiding the Republican caucus through the upcoming debates and ensuring that the Senate can meet its constitutional and fiscal responsibilities.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Supreme Court blocks Trump effort to limit mail‑in voting
content:
Former President Donald Trump has repeatedly voiced criticism of mail‑in voting, describing the practice as vulnerable to fraud and calling for tighter controls. In the weeks leading up to the upcoming midterm elections, Trump and allies have promoted legislation and administrative measures aimed at limiting the use of absentee ballots, including proposals to shorten receipt deadlines, require additional identification, and increase scrutiny of ballot processing.

Election officials and state lawmakers have responded to the pressure by reviewing existing mail‑in voting rules, with several states already enacting modest reforms while others have defended current procedures as secure and legally sound. The heightened focus on absentee voting comes amid broader national debates over election integrity, and observers note that the controversy could influence voter turnout and administrative preparations for the November contests.
author: Al Jazeera

title: UN experts claim Belarus justice system targets Lukashenko opponents
content:
Experts have warned that a coordinated network of courts, police, security services, prosecutors and prison authorities is being used to suppress dissenting voices. The assessment, presented in a recent analysis by independent legal scholars, alleges that these institutions work in concert to curtail the activities of critics, employing legal proceedings, investigations and custodial measures as tools of repression.

The report cites a series of cases in which outspoken individuals faced charges, prolonged pre‑trial detention and restrictive court orders that effectively limited their public engagement. While officials of the implicated agencies have declined to comment on the allegations, human‑rights monitors say the pattern underscores a systemic approach to limiting freedom of expression, prompting calls for further scrutiny and accountability.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Nairobi selected to host 2029 World Athletics Championships
content:
Nairobi has been selected by World Athletics as the host city for the upcoming global track‑and‑field championships, becoming the first African venue to secure the event. The decision, announced on Tuesday, saw the Kenyan capital prevail over rival bids from London, Munich and Rome after a competitive selection process that evaluated infrastructure, legacy plans and regional development goals.

World Athletics President Ulf Lindgren highlighted the significance of the award, noting that the Nairobi bid demonstrated strong governmental support, a clear vision for sustainable sport facilities and a commitment to expanding athletics across the continent. Organisers anticipate that the tournament, slated for 2025, will draw thousands of athletes and spectators, boost tourism and inspire a new generation of African athletes, while also prompting upgrades to existing stadiums and transport networks in the city. The move marks a historic milestone for African sport and underscores World Athletics’ strategy of diversifying host locations worldwide.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Pro-Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil sues Columbia University over alleged racism
content:
Mahmoud Khalil, a former graduate student at Columbia University, filed a civil lawsuit on Tuesday against the institution and its dean, alleging that the university engaged in institutional racism by targeting students who expressed pro‑Palestinian views. The complaint, submitted to the New York State Supreme Court, asserts that Columbia’s administration implemented policies and disciplinary actions that disproportionately affected pro‑Palestine activists, creating a hostile academic environment and violating the plaintiffs’ civil rights. Khalil seeks compensatory damages, injunctive relief to halt the alleged discriminatory practices, and a court order requiring the university to revise its conduct codes and grievance procedures.

The lawsuit arrives amid heightened tensions on college campuses nationwide, where debates over the Israeli‑Palestinian conflict have sparked both student protests and administrative responses. Columbia University has previously issued statements emphasizing its commitment to free expression while condemning hate speech, and the dean has denied any discriminatory intent, asserting that disciplinary measures were applied uniformly. The case will test the university’s policies on political expression and could set precedent for how higher‑education institutions address claims of bias related to campus activism.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Pentagon report details US aircraft and building losses from Iran attacks
content:
The Department of Defense’s Office of Inspector General released a report this week detailing substantial losses suffered by U.S. forces and installations in a key overseas region. The assessment, which examined incidents over the past twelve months, concluded that personnel casualties, equipment degradation, and damage to critical infrastructure have collectively eroded the operational readiness of the units stationed there. According to the findings, a combination of hostile actions, accidental mishaps, and supply-chain shortfalls contributed to the deterioration, prompting concerns about the ability to sustain current mission sets.

In response to the watchdog’s conclusions, senior defense officials indicated that a comprehensive review of force protection measures and logistical support is under way. The report recommends immediate corrective actions, including enhanced security protocols, accelerated repair and replacement programs, and a reassessment of risk management practices. The Pentagon has pledged to incorporate the recommendations into its ongoing strategic planning to mitigate further losses and restore the affected capabilities.
author: Al Jazeera

title: US 10-year Treasury yield hits 19-year high as oil prices rise
content:
The 10‑year U.S. Treasury yield rose to 5.02 percent on Tuesday, marking the first time it has reached that level since the 2007 global financial crisis. The increase was driven by a combination of stronger-than-expected inflation data and the Federal Reserve’s continued emphasis on tightening monetary policy, prompting investors to demand higher yields on government debt.

Higher Treasury yields raise borrowing costs for businesses and consumers, potentially slowing economic activity and influencing mortgage rates, corporate financing, and the broader credit market. Analysts note that the move reflects market expectations of further rate hikes, while also highlighting the sensitivity of Treasury prices to shifts in inflation outlook and policy signals. The yield’s climb underscores ongoing volatility in fixed‑income markets as policymakers navigate the balance between curbing inflation and supporting growth.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Objects on tracks cause major rail disruption in the Netherlands
content:
Train services across several regions were disrupted on Tuesday after unidentified objects were discovered on railway tracks at multiple sites. The incidents prompted immediate safety checks by rail operators, leading to the cancellation of a number of scheduled services and delays to others while crews worked to clear the obstructions and verify track integrity.

Officials from the national rail authority said that teams were dispatched to each affected location and that normal operations were expected to resume once the tracks were deemed safe. Commuters were advised to check real‑time service updates and consider alternative transport options as the disruptions continued into the evening.
author: BBC World

title: Denmark says Russian warship fired flares at military helicopter
content:
Copenhagen – Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said on Tuesday that Russia’s recent actions constitute “reckless” behaviour, urging the international community to hold Moscow accountable. The remarks came after a series of incidents that heightened security concerns in the Baltic region, including reports of unannounced Russian military flights near Danish airspace and the alleged deployment of advanced missile systems in neighboring territories.

The Kremlin has not issued a response to Frederiksen’s accusation, and officials in Moscow declined to comment when approached for a statement. Analysts note that Denmark, a NATO member bordering the Baltic Sea, has been vocal in condemning what it views as destabilising moves by Russia, while the lack of a Russian reply leaves the diplomatic exchange unresolved. The situation remains under close observation by European security agencies.
author: BBC World

title: Mahomes Leads Chiefs to 31-10 Victory Over Broncos
content:
Kansas City’s offense dominated the Denver Broncos on Monday night, handing the visiting team a 31‑10 loss in a game that highlighted both veteran resilience and rookie impact. Patrick Mahomes, who returned from a season‑long recovery after tearing his left ACL, led the Chiefs with two touchdown passes and capped the opening drive with a 15‑yard run, while rookie Kenneth Walker III rushed for 173 yards and two touchdowns on his first game with the franchise.

Mahomes’ performance addressed lingering doubts about the durability of his repaired knee, as he completed every practice of the offseason program and every training‑camp drill before the season’s first game. His two touchdown throws and explosive run set the tone for Kansas City’s offense, which also benefited from Walker’s immediate production. The rookie’s 173‑yard effort, the most by a Chiefs running back in his debut, drew attention and provided a bright spot for the team’s backfield.

The Chiefs’ decisive victory over the Broncos underscores the effectiveness of their offensive strategy and the depth of their roster. With Mahomes proving his knee can withstand the demands of an NFL season and Walker delivering a standout debut, Kansas City appears well positioned to build on this momentum in the weeks ahead.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Daily Football Quizzes Test Your Knowledge
content:
Sports enthusiasts and trivia lovers can sharpen their knowledge today with a trio of quick‑fire challenges. The daily “Ball Knowledge” segment features three distinct quizzes: a “Who Am I?” guessing game, a “Five in Five” rapid‑fire round, and a classic “Brainteaser” puzzle. Each segment is designed to test familiarity with player stats, historical milestones, and game‑changing moments across basketball’s major leagues.

In the “Who Am I?” portion, participants identify a player based on a series of clues about career achievements, signature moves, and notable seasons. The “Five in Five” segment presents five questions in five minutes, covering topics from rookie debuts to championship records. Finally, the “Brainteaser” offers a logic puzzle that requires combining statistical data with contextual clues to solve. All three challenges are available on the network’s website and mobile app, with instant scoring and leaderboards updated in real time.

These daily quizzes aim to engage fans between games and provide a fun, educational way to stay connected to the sport. Participants can track their progress over time and compare scores with friends, making the segment a popular feature among casual and hardcore basketball followers alike.
author: BBC Sport

title: Finn says Pietersen will bring needed challenge to England's white‑ball side
content:
England fast bowler Steven Finn has called for the inclusion of former England captain Kevin Pietersen in the national white‑ball squad, arguing that Pietersen’s blunt and forthright approach would add a needed edge to the side. Finn said that the timing is ideal as England look to strengthen their limited‑overs lineup ahead of the upcoming series against the West Indies and the ICC World Cup.

Pietersen, who has returned to international cricket after a long absence, is known for his aggressive batting and outspoken personality. Finn highlighted Pietersen’s ability to pressure opposition bowlers and his experience in high‑pressure situations, noting that these attributes could complement England’s current white‑ball attack and provide a new dimension to the team’s strategy. The call comes as England’s white‑ball side has struggled to find consistent form in the one‑day format, prompting selectors to consider fresh options.

If Pietersen is recalled, it would signal a shift in England’s approach to limited‑overs cricket, blending experience with a more confrontational style. The selectors will weigh Finn’s recommendation against the team’s long‑term plans, but the suggestion underscores a broader debate about how best to build a competitive white‑ball side in the modern era.
author: BBC Sport

title: Enzo Maresca Takes Over Manchester City
content:
Enzo Maresca has stepped into the role of Manchester City manager after the departure of Pep Guardiola, a transition that many pundits deemed daunting. The Italian, who previously guided Inter Milan and the Italy national team, was appointed in late May following a brief search that saw several high‑profile candidates decline the offer. City’s board cited Maresca’s tactical acumen and experience in European competitions as key reasons for their choice, hoping he can maintain the club’s competitive edge while injecting fresh ideas.

In the early stages of his tenure, Maresca has already begun to imprint his philosophy on the squad. He has retained the core of Guardiola’s personnel, making only strategic adjustments to the attacking lineup and emphasizing a more fluid, possession‑based approach. Early pre‑season fixtures have seen City secure convincing wins, with Maresca’s side displaying disciplined defending and rapid transitions. Analysts note that his emphasis on player development and tactical flexibility could help the club navigate the congested Premier League and Champions League calendars.

While the full impact of Maresca’s leadership will unfold over the course of the season, his initial performances suggest that he is handling the pressure of succeeding a football legend with a calm, methodical approach. If the early momentum continues, City may be poised to sustain its domestic dominance while pursuing new ambitions on the European stage.
author: BBC Sport

title: Attorney General Todd Blanche to Brief Reporters in White House Rose Garden
content:
Attorney General Todd Blanche is scheduled to brief reporters in the White House Rose Garden on Tuesday, marking his entry into a role that has traditionally been held by the White House press secretary. The announcement comes as the administration seeks to maintain continuity in its communications strategy after the departure of former press secretary Karoline Leavitt.

A White House spokesperson confirmed to NewsNation, the sister network of The Hill, that Blanche will address the press in the Rose Garden, a venue commonly used for official briefings. While the Attorney General’s primary duties involve overseeing the Department of Justice, his appearance signals the administration’s intent to keep the press closely informed on legal and policy matters. The briefing is expected to cover recent developments in the administration’s agenda and to answer questions from journalists covering the White House.

The briefing will provide reporters with a direct line to the Attorney General’s perspective on current issues, reinforcing the administration’s commitment to transparency. As the latest official to step into a role traditionally occupied by the press secretary, Blanche’s appearance underscores the importance of clear communication between the White House and the media.
author: The Hill

title: House Rules Committee Approves Bipartisan Russia Sanctions Bill
content:
The House Rules Committee approved a bipartisan bill on Monday that would expand U.S. sanctions against Russia in the wake of its ongoing war in Ukraine. The legislation, championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, would empower the President to target individuals and entities working on behalf of the Russian government that are believed to be obstructing peace negotiations and violating negotiated ceasefire agreements.

Under the proposed measure, the President would be granted authority to impose penalties on a broader range of Russian actors, including those who facilitate military support or diplomatic interference aimed at stalling diplomatic progress with Ukraine. The bill reflects growing bipartisan concern that current sanctions are insufficient to deter Russia’s aggressive actions and to ensure compliance with international agreements.

If enacted, the legislation would signal a stronger U.S. stance on the conflict and provide a clearer legal framework for punitive actions against those undermining peace efforts in Ukraine. The House Rules Committee’s approval moves the measure closer to full congressional debate and potential passage.
author: The Hill

title: Nancy Mace urges public execution of Lindsay Clancy
content:
Rep. Nancy Mace (R‑S.C.) told TMZ on Monday that Lindsay Clancy, a Massachusetts woman facing a new trial for the alleged murder of her three children, should be publicly executed.  Mace said, “Her children are dead, she should be dead too,” and later added that the death penalty “should be public.”  The remarks came as Clancy’s case moves forward in the state’s court system.

Clancy is accused of killing her three children in 2019, and her defense team has requested a new trial after the original proceedings ended in a mistrial.  Massachusetts abolished the death penalty in 1984 and does not allow public executions, so Mace’s comments are not aligned with state law.  The statement was widely reported by media outlets that covered the interview with the congresswoman.

Mace’s comments have drawn attention to the broader debate over capital punishment and the legal limits of public executions in the United States.  While the case remains pending, the congresswoman’s remarks highlight the ongoing tensions between political rhetoric and the legal framework governing criminal penalties.
author: The Hill

title: Police Commissioner Mulls Canceling Colin Sutton's 127-Show Tour
content:
Colin Sutton, the rising star of the true‑crime performance circuit, is slated to stage his signature show 127 times between January and November. The series, billed as an immersive exploration of notorious cases, will run across a mix of theatres and intimate venues, drawing on Sutton’s reputation for blending investigative storytelling with theatrical flair.

The schedule, announced by Sutton’s management team, spans 11 months and includes 127 dates that will take the performer from major city centres to regional theatres. Each performance promises a deep dive into a different criminal case, featuring archival material, reenactments, and interactive audience participation. The tour’s extensive run underscores the growing appetite for live true‑crime entertainment and positions Sutton as a key figure in the genre’s theatrical expansion.

With the tour set to conclude in late November, Sutton’s ambitious 127‑performance run is expected to solidify his standing as a leading voice in live true‑crime storytelling, while offering fans a comprehensive, month‑by‑month journey through some of history’s most compelling crimes.
author: BBC Politics

title: UK Minister Calls for Heeding AI Developers' Warnings
content:
Louise Haigh, the Labour MP and former Minister for Trade, will speak on Tuesday at the Trades Union Congress (TUC) Congress in London, addressing growing concerns about artificial intelligence safety. The TUC Congress, the annual gathering of the UK’s largest trade union federation, will feature a series of panels on technology and the future of work, with Haigh’s remarks slated to follow the keynote address by the TUC General Secretary.

In her comments, Haigh is expected to outline the potential risks posed by AI systems in the workplace, including job displacement, data privacy issues, and the need for robust regulatory frameworks. She will call for stronger safeguards and greater transparency from technology firms, and will highlight the TUC’s interest in ensuring that workers’ rights are protected as automation becomes increasingly pervasive. The discussion will also touch on the role of public policy in balancing innovation with social responsibility.

Haigh’s participation underscores the TUC’s commitment to shaping national policy on emerging technologies. By bringing the conversation to the forefront of the union’s agenda, the Congress aims to influence lawmakers and industry stakeholders to adopt measures that promote safe, inclusive, and accountable AI deployment across the UK economy.
author: BBC Politics

title: Reform UK Receives £72m Donation, Sparks Debate on Political Funding
content:
The £72 million that has just entered Reform UK’s bank account is already reshaping the Westminster conversation about the nexus of money and politics.  The sum, which came from a series of high‑profile donors and a recent fundraising event, is being earmarked for the party’s campaign infrastructure and policy research.  Critics argue that the influx could give Reform UK an outsized influence on parliamentary debates, while supporters claim it is simply a necessary investment to compete in a crowded political landscape.

The money has prompted a flurry of parliamentary questions and media scrutiny.  Members of the opposition have called for a review of campaign finance rules, citing concerns that large private contributions may undermine public trust.  Reform UK’s leadership, meanwhile, has pledged to use the funds transparently and to maintain strict compliance with the Electoral Commission’s reporting requirements.  The debate underscores a broader national reckoning over how political parties are financed and how that finance shapes policy priorities.

In short, the £72 million injection is more than a budget boost; it is a catalyst for renewed debate on campaign finance reform.  As Westminster grapples with the implications, lawmakers and the public alike are watching to see whether this windfall will prompt stricter regulations or simply intensify the existing dynamics between money and political power.
author: BBC Politics

title: New Fertility Calculator Estimates Natural Conception Chances
content:
Scientists at the University of Aberdeen in partnership with NHS Grampian have released a new predictive tool that estimates a couple’s likelihood of conceiving naturally before they decide to pursue in‑vitro fertilisation (IVF). The software, built on a database of thousands of fertility cases, integrates key variables such as maternal age, ovarian reserve markers, sperm quality and previous pregnancy history to generate a personalised probability score.

Early validation studies show the model correctly identifies couples with a high chance of spontaneous conception in 78 % of cases and those unlikely to conceive naturally in 85 % of cases, according to data released by the research team. By providing an evidence‑based estimate, the tool aims to help clinicians and patients weigh the risks, costs and emotional toll of IVF against the realistic possibility of natural pregnancy, potentially reducing unnecessary treatment cycles.

If adopted widely, the application could streamline fertility care pathways and inform shared decision‑making. The developers plan to integrate the tool into routine fertility clinic assessments and to conduct further trials to refine its predictive accuracy across diverse populations.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Scotland Updates Infection Control Guidelines Based on Pandemic Evidence
content:
Scotland has become the first country in the world to revise its health‑care respiratory‑disease prevention guidelines using data collected during the COVID‑19 pandemic. The new policy framework, announced by the Scottish Government’s Health and Social Care Director, draws on a recent study conducted by the University of Bristol in partnership with Bristol NHS Foundation Trust.

The study, which analysed infection rates and transmission pathways in hospital wards across the United Kingdom, identified key factors that reduced the spread of respiratory pathogens. Findings highlighted the effectiveness of enhanced ventilation, targeted use of high‑efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filtration, and refined patient cohorting strategies. Based on these insights, Scotland’s updated guidelines now mandate stricter ventilation standards, expanded use of portable air‑cleaning units, and revised protocols for patient isolation and staff movement within clinical settings.

By integrating pandemic‑era evidence into its health‑care policies, Scotland aims to strengthen infection control and protect both patients and staff from future respiratory outbreaks. The move signals a broader shift toward data‑driven public‑health decision‑making and positions the nation as a leader in evidence‑based health‑care practice.
author: Medical Xpress

title: AI advances improve reliability of medical image analysis
content:
Machine learning, a subset of artificial intelligence that allows computers to learn from data and generate predictive insights, is becoming a foundational technology in modern health‑care systems. By processing large volumes of clinical information, these algorithms can support clinicians in making data‑driven decisions, a shift that is reflected in recent deployments across hospitals and research institutions worldwide.

In practice, machine‑learning tools are applied to a range of clinical tasks, including automated disease diagnosis, forecasting disease progression, optimizing treatment plans, and continuous patient monitoring. The integration of these capabilities promises to enhance diagnostic accuracy, streamline therapeutic workflows, and enable more personalized care, positioning the technology as a critical component of future health‑care delivery.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study finds nearly one-third of college BORG drinkers report blackouts
content:
A new study published in the *Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs* by researchers at Rutgers University has identified a rapidly spreading college drinking practice known as the “blackout rage gallon” (BORG). The trend involves students mixing large quantities of hard liquor with sugary mixers in a single container, encouraging rapid consumption that can quickly lead to severe intoxication and blackout episodes. Survey data collected from more than 2,000 undergraduate respondents across 30 campuses indicate that BORG use has risen sharply over the past two years, with roughly 18 % of surveyed students reporting having tried the drink at least once.

The researchers found that participants who consumed a BORG were significantly more likely to engage in binge‑drinking behaviors, experience alcohol poisoning, and suffer injuries related to impaired judgment. The study links the trend to higher rates of emergency‑room visits, academic disruption, and increased risk of long‑term alcohol use disorders. Authors recommend that university health services and campus authorities implement targeted education campaigns and stricter monitoring of large‑volume alcohol purchases to mitigate the growing public‑health threat posed by the BORG phenomenon.
author: Medical Xpress

title: State pension set to rise 3.9% in April
content:
The government announced that the state pension will be increased by the highest of three measures – average wage growth, consumer‑price inflation or a minimum of 2.5 % – a formula known as the “triple lock”. The policy, which has been applied annually since 2010, is intended to protect pensioners’ purchasing power by ensuring that the uplift matches the strongest indicator of rising living standards.

Under the triple‑lock mechanism, the Department for Work and Pensions will compare the latest figures for earnings growth and the Consumer Price Index and apply the greatest of the three percentages to the basic state pension. If wage growth or inflation falls below 2.5 %, the pension will still rise by that minimum rate. The approach is expected to raise the weekly pension by the determined percentage from April, increasing the cost of the scheme for the Treasury while providing a predictable, inflation‑linked benefit for retirees.
author: BBC Business

title: Dense Galaxies Create Bubble in Early Universe
content:
The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has begun delivering its first scientific data, a milestone that underscores the perseverance of the scientific community and the agency’s long‑term commitment to the project. After years of development marked by significant cost overruns and repeated budgetary concerns, the telescope’s launch and early observations confirm that the mission’s ambitious goals are now being realized.

JWST’s journey to orbit was fraught with financial and political challenges. The project exceeded its original budget by a large margin, prompting scrutiny from lawmakers and the public. In 2011, congressional hearings brought the program to the brink of cancellation, with several budget cuts and program reviews threatening to halt the launch. Despite these setbacks, continued advocacy by NASA officials, the scientific community, and international partners secured the necessary funding and support, allowing the telescope to proceed to launch and subsequent commissioning.

With its first science results now streaming in, JWST demonstrates that the investment in overcoming these obstacles has paid off. The data already being released promise to transform our understanding of the early universe, exoplanet atmospheres, and the formation of stars and galaxies, validating the perseverance that kept the mission alive.
author: Phys.org

title: Australia urged to intensify climate action as study warns 1.5°C threshold breach
content:
Global climate models released this week indicate that the world is on track to exceed the 1.5 °C warming limit established by the 2015 Paris Agreement within the next five years. The projections, compiled by an international consortium of scientists, incorporate recent temperature trends, greenhouse‑gas emissions trajectories, and updated climate sensitivity estimates. The analysis underscores that, even with current mitigation pledges, cumulative carbon dioxide concentrations are poised to surpass the threshold that the agreement identified as the point beyond which climate risks become markedly more severe.

The anticipated breach carries a range of high‑impact consequences. Accelerated melting of polar ice sheets is projected to contribute to sea‑level rise at rates faster than previously modeled, increasing the vulnerability of coastal communities worldwide. In addition, ocean warming is expected to drive widespread coral bleaching, with many reef systems projected to lose their vibrant coloration and structural complexity, effectively turning them into “ghostly white” ecosystems. The report calls for immediate, scaled‑up emissions reductions to narrow the gap between pledged actions and the pathway required to keep warming below the critical 1.5 °C limit.
author: Phys.org

title: MSU team to study 1946 Alaska earthquake fault linked to historic tsunami
content:
A massive tsunami that struck Hawaii, Alaska, Washington and Oregon eight decades ago was triggered by a powerful earthquake off the coast of Alaska. The event, which generated waves up to 30 feet high, caused widespread damage and loss of life across the Pacific Northwest and the Hawaiian Islands. Recent research suggests that the tsunami’s source was a previously unrecognized underwater fault system that ruptured during the 1944 earthquake.

In response, a team from Michigan State University is launching a comprehensive study of the fault system that produced the 1944 tsunami. Using a combination of seismic imaging, bathymetric mapping and numerical modeling, the researchers aim to reconstruct the fault’s geometry, slip history and potential for future activity. By comparing the 1944 rupture with modern seismic records, the team hopes to assess whether the fault remains active and could pose a risk to coastal communities today.

The project’s findings will inform hazard assessments for the Pacific Northwest and the Hawaiian Islands, helping authorities refine evacuation plans and infrastructure resilience. If the fault is still capable of generating large earthquakes, the study will provide critical data for updating tsunami warning systems and ensuring that coastal populations are better prepared for a repeat of the 1944 disaster.
author: Phys.org

title: New precise electroweak calculation challenges standard model
content:
A collaboration of theorists from several international institutes has announced the most precise calculation to date of the electroweak interaction, the force that unifies electromagnetism and the weak nuclear force. Using a combination of high‑order perturbative techniques and advanced lattice simulations, the team reduced the theoretical uncertainty on key parameters such as the weak mixing angle and the W‑boson mass to a level comparable with the most accurate experimental measurements.

The refined results tighten the Standard Model’s predictions for processes that have previously shown small but persistent deviations, including the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon and recent discrepancies in W‑boson mass determinations. By narrowing the gap between theory and observation, the calculation provides a more stringent test of the model’s internal consistency and limits the parameter space for possible new physics scenarios, such as supersymmetry or additional gauge bosons.

Physicists say the achievement offers a critical benchmark for upcoming experiments at the Large Hadron Collider and future facilities, where even finer measurements will be possible. Continued interplay between high‑precision theory and experiment is expected to either confirm the Standard Model’s robustness or reveal concrete signs of physics beyond its current framework.
author: New Scientist

title: Deep West African coral reef found alive after 60 years
content:
Scientists have confirmed that a coral reef off the coast of Benin, long presumed dead after surveys conducted more than six decades ago, is in fact alive. Underwater cameras deployed at depths exceeding 50 meters captured vibrant coral patches teeming with a variety of fish species, overturning earlier assessments that the reef had succumbed to degradation. The discovery was made during a recent exploratory mission that aimed to verify the condition of the seabed in the region, and the footage showed healthy-looking colonies with no visible signs of bleaching or disease.

The finding suggests that West Africa’s coastal waters may host additional, undocumented reef systems that have escaped scientific scrutiny. Researchers note that the presence of a thriving reef in an area previously thought to lack viable coral could prompt renewed surveys and targeted conservation efforts across the Gulf of Guinea. Ongoing analysis of the video data and subsequent sampling will help determine the extent of the reef, its biodiversity, and its resilience, informing future marine management strategies in the region.
author: Science Daily

title: Ancient DNA shows plague infected Siberian hunter‑gatherers 5,500 years ago
content:
Ancient DNA analysis has confirmed that Yersinia pestis was responsible for lethal infections among hunter‑gatherer groups in Siberia around 5,500 years ago, predating the rise of cities and the flea‑borne epidemics traditionally associated with the Black Death. Researchers extracted bacterial genomes from skeletal remains uncovered in the Lake Baikal region and identified them as early‑branching plague strains, establishing that the disease was already active in human populations long before settled agriculture.

The prehistoric Y. pestis variants carried a specific genetic element that amplifies host immune responses, potentially triggering severe, often fatal, inflammation. This virulence factor, absent in many later strains, suggests that early plague outbreaks could have been especially deadly. The findings broaden the timeline of plague’s evolutionary history, indicating that its impact on human health began in nomadic societies and offering new perspectives for studying pathogen adaptation and ancient disease dynamics.
author: Science Daily

title: APOD September 15, 2026: Daytime Eclipse Shows Moon Occulting Venus
content:
The Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD) released its September 15, 2026 entry, continuing the long‑running NASA‑backed initiative that showcases a new image of the universe each day accompanied by a brief, astronomer‑written explanation. Today’s selection features a striking daytime photograph of a celestial object or phenomenon, illustrating the program’s commitment to presenting both spectacular visuals and accessible scientific context to a global audience. The image, posted alongside a concise description, highlights the current observational focus of professional and amateur astronomers alike.

APOD, now in its third decade, maintains an extensive archive that can be searched by date, keyword, or subject, providing educators, researchers, and the public with a searchable repository of astronomical imagery. By delivering daily content that blends visual appeal with expert commentary, the service reinforces public interest in space science and supports informal education worldwide. The September 15 posting adds another entry to this growing catalog, underscoring APOD’s role as a reliable conduit for disseminating contemporary astronomical discoveries.
author: NASA News

title: Former FTC Chair Lina Khan urges use of 1934 antitrust law against AI CEOs
content:
Former Federal Trade Commission chair Lina Khan has called on U.S. policymakers to loosen the regulatory “handcuffs” placed on chief executives of artificial‑intelligence firms, invoking a 1934 legal precedent that limited government interference in corporate leadership. In a recent op‑ed, Khan argued that the current antitrust and securities‑law environment, which subjects AI CEOs to heightened scrutiny and potential liability, could stifle innovation and delay the deployment of emerging technologies. She cited the 1934 case of *United States v. United Shoe Machinery Corp.*, in which the Supreme Court rejected overly aggressive government control over corporate governance, to illustrate that historical jurisprudence supports a more restrained approach.

Khan’s appeal arrives amid a wave of investigations into major AI companies, with the FTC and the Department of Justice examining potential market‑power abuses and data‑privacy concerns. Industry groups have welcomed the suggestion, saying it could provide clearer guidance for executive decision‑making, while consumer‑advocacy organizations warn that easing constraints might reduce accountability. The commentary generated notable attention on the Hacker News forum, where the linked discussion earned 131 points and 59 comments, reflecting a broader debate over the balance between regulatory oversight and the rapid growth of the AI sector.
author: Hacker News

title: Linux From Scratch post receives 60 points on Hacker News
content:
Linux From Scratch (LFS), a long‑standing project that provides step‑by‑step instructions for building a custom Linux system from source code, has attracted renewed attention on the technology news aggregator Hacker News. A post linking to the official LFS website (https://www.linuxfromscratch.org) received 60 points and generated 22 comments, indicating significant community interest in the guide’s latest updates and its relevance for developers and hobbyists seeking deeper insight into Linux internals.

The discussion on Hacker News highlighted recent revisions to the LFS documentation, including updated package versions, improved build scripts, and expanded support for modern hardware architectures. Participants noted the educational value of constructing a Linux system from the ground up, emphasizing how the process reinforces understanding of system components, dependency management, and compilation techniques. The thread also referenced related projects such as Beyond Linux From Scratch (BLFS), which extends the base system with additional software, and shared experiences from users who successfully completed the build on various platforms.

Overall, the surge in engagement reflects continued enthusiasm for hands‑on Linux learning resources. The LFS project’s ongoing maintenance and the active dialogue among its users suggest that the initiative remains a pertinent tool for both newcomers and seasoned engineers aiming to deepen their mastery of Linux system construction.
author: Hacker News

title: US Military Confirms Deployment of On‑Orbit Space Weapons
content:
The Department of Defense announced that the United States now possesses on‑orbit space control weapons designed to protect the joint force. The new capability, described in a recent briefing, enables the military to engage, neutralize, or otherwise mitigate threats to U.S. and allied space assets while they remain in orbit.

According to the statement, the weapons system integrates with existing satellite constellations and command‑and‑control networks, providing a rapid response option against potential adversarial actions in the space domain. Officials indicated that the development aligns with broader strategic objectives to ensure freedom of operation for U.S. forces across all warfighting environments, and they emphasized that the technology will be employed in accordance with applicable laws and regulations.
author: Ars Technica

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang receives live call from Donald Trump
content:
NVIDIA chief executive Jensen Huang fielded a live telephone call from former President Donald Trump during a technology conference on Thursday, marking an unusual direct dialogue between the AI industry leader and the former commander‑in‑chief. The call, which was streamed to attendees and later posted online, focused on Trump’s interest in artificial‑intelligence developments and potential collaborations with the chipmaker. While the conversation itself centered on policy and technical questions, viewers also noted the device Huang used to answer the call, sparking separate commentary about the phone’s make and model.

Industry observers said the attention given to the handset underscored the growing visibility of personal technology choices among high‑profile executives, especially when they intersect with major public events. The incident highlights both the expanding role of AI in political discourse and the heightened scrutiny of the tools used by corporate leaders in such engagements. No further statements have been released by NVIDIA or the Trump campaign regarding the content of the discussion.
author: TechCrunch

title: England and Wales allow digital ID biometric age checks in pubs and bars
content:
New legislation that takes effect this week permits licensed premises in England and Wales to use biometric technology to verify that customers are over 18, while still allowing traditional plastic identification. Under the law, pubs, off‑licences, nightclubs and restaurants may accept a digital age‑verification method in which a patron downloads an app, scans their face with a smartphone camera and receives a QR code that confirms their age based on stored proof‑of‑age data.

The government’s push to modernise age checks also includes consideration of a finger‑vein scanning device that could authenticate a drinker’s age, although that technology has not yet received regulatory approval. The new framework aims to streamline the verification process for younger drinkers, but retailers are required to continue accepting conventional photo IDs until any additional digital solutions are formally authorised.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Alex Saab to plead guilty in U.S. money laundering case
content:
A man identified only as Saab has been charged with a single count of money laundering in connection with an alleged scheme to establish fictitious companies and falsify shipping documents. Court records indicate that the indictment links him to a broader conspiracy that purportedly used the sham entities to conceal illicit financial transactions and manipulate trade data.

Saab is scheduled to appear before a Miami federal judge on Tuesday for a change‑of‑plea hearing, where he will be given the opportunity to enter a plea to the charge. The hearing will determine whether the case proceeds to trial or if a plea agreement is reached, concluding the current phase of the investigation into the purported fraudulent corporate and shipping activities.
author: Euronews

title: September 15 2026 News Bulletin: Europe and Global Highlights
content:
September 15, 2026 – A broad sweep of headlines from Europe and beyond highlights a day of political negotiations, economic data releases, cultural milestones and travel developments. In Brussels, EU leaders convened for a summit aimed at tightening the bloc’s 2030 climate targets, proposing a 15 percent increase in renewable‑energy subsidies and a phased ban on coal‑fired power plants by 2029. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom’s newly formed coalition government presented its first fiscal plan, projecting a modest 0.4 percent GDP growth for the year and earmarking £12 billion for infrastructure upgrades in the Midlands. In Germany, the Federal Statistical Office reported a 2.1 percent rise in industrial production in August, driven chiefly by the automotive sector’s rebound after supply‑chain disruptions.

Across the cultural and entertainment spectrum, France opened the Cannes‑style “Mediterranean Film Festival” in Nice, showcasing 45 international films and awarding the Grand Prix to a Spanish director for a documentary on renewable energy. The travel industry noted a surge in bookings to the Baltic states, with Estonia reporting a 12 percent increase in tourist arrivals compared with the same period last year, attributed to new visa‑free agreements with several Asian markets. These developments collectively underscore a period of strategic policy shifts, modest economic optimism and vibrant cultural exchange shaping the European landscape today.
author: Euronews

title: Supreme Court blocks Trump bid to restrict mail voting
content:
A federal court ruling on Thursday upheld the long‑standing practice of mailing ballots to voters, permitting states to maintain the same procedures they have employed for years. The decision comes amid ongoing legal challenges to the expansion of absentee voting, and it affirms that the existing mail‑in systems remain consistent with constitutional and statutory requirements.

By preserving the current framework, the ruling ensures that the method, which accounts for roughly one‑third of all votes cast in recent elections, will continue to be used in upcoming contests. Election officials across the affected states said they will proceed with their established mailing schedules and verification protocols, while observers note that the decision may influence future debates over voting accessibility and election integrity.
author: Euronews

title: Serbian university students form new party to contest October parliamentary election
content:
Serbia’s university students officially launched their electoral campaign on Monday, 14 September, registering as a political contender for the early parliamentary elections set for 25 October. The move marks the first time a coordinated student bloc has entered the national race, positioning itself as a direct challenger to President Aleksandar Vučić and the ruling Serbian Progressive Party, which has dominated the country’s political landscape for over a decade.

The students’ entry adds a new dimension to a contest already characterized by concerns over media freedom, economic reforms and Serbia’s relationship with the European Union. Analysts note that the timing of the registration, just weeks before the vote, could influence voter sentiment, particularly among younger constituents. As the campaign period unfolds, the student platform’s impact on the broader opposition coalition and its ability to mobilize support will be closely monitored ahead of the October ballot.
author: Euronews

title: Israeli strikes kill at least two, injure several in Gaza
content:
At least two people were killed and several others injured in Israeli airstrikes that hit multiple locations across the Gaza Strip on Monday, 14 September, according to hospital and health officials monitoring the situation. The casualties were reported by the Gaza Ministry of Health, which said the attacks struck residential neighborhoods and a nearby medical facility, overwhelming local emergency services as they responded to the influx of wounded.

Health authorities said the strikes were part of a broader campaign of aerial operations launched by Israel in response to recent escalations in the region. Hospitals across Gaza reported an increase in trauma cases, with medical staff working under strained conditions to treat the injured. The latest figures bring the death toll in the ongoing conflict to a higher level, underscoring the heightened intensity of hostilities and the humanitarian challenges faced by the enclave’s civilian population.
author: Euronews

title: Supreme Court denies Trump's bid to limit mail ballots before midterms
content:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday denied former President Donald Trump’s request to impose new restrictions on mail‑in ballots for the upcoming November midterm elections. The Court’s refusal to grant a temporary injunction means that states may continue to follow the voting procedures already in place, without the additional limitations sought by the Trump campaign.

Election officials had warned that the proposed changes, introduced just weeks before the election, could jeopardize the timely distribution and processing of absentee ballots. By leaving existing rules intact, the Court’s decision averts potential disruptions to ballot delivery and allows states to proceed with their current mail‑voting systems as voters head toward the midterm polls.
author: France 24

title: NATO jets shoot down drone over Lithuania
content:
NATO fighter jets intercepted and destroyed an unmanned aerial vehicle that entered Lithuanian airspace, the Baltic nation’s president announced on Tuesday. The incident marks the latest security breach on the alliance’s eastern frontier amid heightened tensions linked to Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine. Lithuanian authorities reported that the drone was detected by national radar and that NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission dispatched aircraft to neutralize the threat within minutes.

The shoot‑down underscores NATO’s continued commitment to protect the airspace of its member states bordering Russia, a policy reinforced after a series of similar incursions in the region over the past year. While officials have not identified the drone’s origin, they emphasized that the response was conducted in accordance with established NATO protocols. The alliance reiterated that it remains vigilant in monitoring and defending its eastern flank as the conflict in Ukraine persists.
author: France 24

title: Venezuela to attend G20 energy talks in Houston after US invitation
content:
A Venezuelan delegation is set to participate in the G20 energy ministers’ meeting in Houston this week, a gathering convened amid sharply rising oil prices and heightened concerns over global energy security. The talks come as the conflict in the Middle East continues to disrupt supply chains, prompting the United States and other major producers to seek additional sources to stabilize markets.

The presence of Caracas officials reflects the Trump administration’s effort to deepen energy cooperation with Venezuela, including initiatives aimed at increasing Venezuelan oil production despite longstanding sanctions. By integrating Venezuela into the G20 dialogue, Washington hopes to expand the pool of available crude and mitigate the impact of geopolitical tensions on worldwide energy supplies.
author: France 24

title: Pentagon inspector general reports US ammunition shortfall linked to Iran war
content:
The Pentagon’s inspector general reported that the United States military is confronting a significant ammunition shortfall linked to its ongoing conflict in Iran, a war that has already incurred an estimated $33.4 billion in expenses during its first four months. The audit highlights supply chain strains and heightened demand for munitions as operational tempos increase, prompting concerns among defense planners about the sustainability of current stockpiles and the potential impact on readiness across multiple theaters.

Separately, Saudi officials on Tuesday accused Yemen’s Houthi rebels of deploying ballistic missiles and drones in attacks that injured 13 civilians in the kingdom’s southern region. The allegations come amid a broader pattern of cross‑border hostilities that have intensified regional security challenges. Authorities are monitoring the situation closely, and updates continue to be provided through a liveblog covering the latest developments.
author: France 24

title: Ballon d’Or contenders Mbappé, Yamal, Dembélé and Kane launch campaign ahead of vote
content:
With two weeks remaining before the Ballon d’Or voting deadline, the sport’s top nominees have intensified their outreach to the journalists, national team coaches, and captains who comprise the award’s electorate. The annual accolade, administered by France Football, opens its ballot in early October and closes on 15 October, after which votes are tallied for a ceremony scheduled for late November. Current frontrunners—including the Premier League’s Erling Haaland, Paris Saint‑Germain’s Kylian Mbappé, and Inter Milan’s Lautaro Martínez—are leveraging club platforms and personal media channels to highlight their season‑long performances, while former winners such as Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo have issued statements underscoring their continued relevance in the competition.

Campaign activities this week have featured coordinated press releases from the players’ respective clubs, targeted social‑media posts emphasizing key statistics, and a series of interview appearances aimed at reinforcing each candidate’s impact in domestic leagues and European tournaments. National team representatives have also contributed endorsements, noting the contenders’ contributions in recent international fixtures. As the voting window narrows, the final tally will be compiled and the winner announced at the November ceremony, concluding one of football’s most closely watched annual award processes.
author: France 24

title: US munitions shortages revealed in Pentagon report amid Iran conflict
content:
The Pentagon’s internal watchdog warned on Monday that the U.S. military is confronting shortages of several critical munitions as it works to rebuild stockpiles depleted by the ongoing conflict with Iran and by persistent industrial bottlenecks. The report, issued by the Defense Department’s Office of the Inspector General, detailed gaps in ammunition inventories for artillery, rockets and other weapons systems, citing delayed production and supply‑chain constraints that have hampered replenishment efforts.

The findings stand in contrast to statements made by President Donald Trump, who recently claimed that the nation’s ammunition supplies are “virtually unlimited.” The watchdog’s assessment underscores the challenges of maintaining adequate munitions levels amid heightened operational demands and highlights the need for accelerated manufacturing and logistical coordination to address the shortfall.
author: France 24

title: Panama Canal to reduce traffic again as El Niño‑related drought worsens
content:
The Panama Canal announced another round of traffic restrictions this week as an intensifying drought, linked to the El Niño climate pattern, drives water levels to historically low points. The canal, which accommodates roughly 5 percent of worldwide maritime trade and about 40 percent of U.S. container shipments, will limit the number of vessels that can transit each day, extending the previously imposed reductions that began earlier this year. Officials said the cuts are necessary to preserve the reservoir that powers the canal’s lock system, which relies on fresh water to lift ships between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

The new limitations are expected to increase transit times and freight costs for shippers that favor the canal for its ability to shorten routes between Asia and the United States. Companies that previously saved days and millions of dollars by avoiding the longer journey around Cape Horn may need to reroute or delay cargo, potentially tightening supply chains that already face pressures from global demand. The canal authority indicated that the restrictions will remain in place until water levels recover, underscoring the broader vulnerability of critical trade infrastructure to climate‑driven weather events.
author: Guardian World

title: DRC Ebola outbreak peaks as infection rates decline
content:
Almost 3,500 people have died since the Ebola outbreak was declared in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in May, and health authorities announced this week that the epidemic has reached its peak. Officials reported a measurable decline in the number of new infections, marking the first sustained slowdown in transmission since the crisis began. The World Health Organization and the Congolese Ministry of Health have intensified vaccination campaigns, contact tracing, and community engagement to curb further spread, while emphasizing that the virus remains active in several provinces.

Experts caution that the reduction in case numbers does not signal the end of the threat and call for continued vigilance and resources to maintain control over the outbreak. They stress the importance of sustaining laboratory capacity, safe burial practices, and rapid response teams to prevent resurgence, especially in hard‑to‑reach areas. As the epidemic enters a critical phase, authorities aim to consolidate gains made while preparing for the long‑term management of Ebola in the region.
author: Guardian World

title: US rejects many Afrikaner refugee applications after Trump announcement
content:
Washington, D.C. – The United States’ refugee program for Afrikaners, launched after President Donald Trump announced in February 2025 that the country would accept white South Africans fleeing alleged persecution, is showing early signs of deceleration. The initiative, promoted as a response to claims of a “white genocide” in South Africa, initially attracted significant interest from white South Africans who perceived themselves as victims of systemic racism. Since the program’s inception, however, immigration officials have turned down dozens of applications, citing insufficient evidence that applicants meet the criteria for refugee status under U.S. law.

The recent wave of denials has left many prospective refugees uncertain about their options, as the promised pathway to safety appears increasingly constrained. Critics of the program argue that the “white genocide” narrative lacks substantiation, while supporters contend that the rejections reflect procedural hurdles rather than a shift in policy. The U.S. State Department has not released detailed statistics on the number of applications processed or the specific reasons for refusals, and it has indicated that each case will continue to be evaluated on an individual basis.
author: Guardian World

title: Supreme Court blocks Trump effort to tighten mail-in voting rules
content:
The U.S. Supreme Court on Tuesday denied former President Donald Trump’s request to impose stricter mail‑in voting requirements before the nation’s upcoming midterm elections. The Court, in a brief order, declined to grant a temporary stay that would have halted the implementation of existing absentee‑ballot procedures in several swing states, leaving current rules in place for the November vote.

The decision follows a lower‑court ruling that had upheld state‑level standards for verifying mail‑in ballots, a measure the Trump campaign argued was insufficient to prevent fraud. By refusing to intervene, the high court effectively maintains the status quo, allowing states to continue using their established mail‑in voting processes as they prepare for what is expected to be a highly contested midterm cycle.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Trump calls Nvidia CEO during live event to dismiss AI concerns
content:
President Donald J. Trump placed an unexpected phone call to Nvidia Corp. chief executive Jensen Huang during a live‑streamed event, raising concerns about the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence. The call, which interrupted the presentation of Nvidia’s latest graphics processing units, was brief but highlighted the administration’s growing focus on AI safety and regulatory oversight.

In the conversation, Trump asked Huang about the potential risks of increasingly powerful AI models and inquired whether Nvidia was collaborating with U.S. agencies to address national‑security implications. Huang emphasized the company’s commitment to responsible development and noted ongoing partnerships with government bodies on research and standards. The call reflects heightened political scrutiny of the AI sector, as lawmakers and executives alike debate frameworks to balance innovation with public safety.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Crowds gather at Indian temple for sacred henna ritual
content:
Drone footage captured a throng of people gathering at a temple in northern India where unmarried individuals line up to receive a sacred application of henna, a ritual believed to improve prospects of finding a marital partner. The aerial images, released by local authorities, show long queues extending beyond the temple’s main entrance as volunteers and priests prepare the ceremonial space for the event, which takes place annually during an auspicious period in the Hindu calendar.

The ceremony, rooted in longstanding cultural practices that associate henna with marriage blessings, involves a priest applying a specific design that participants consider a talisman for love. Organisers reported that the event attracts several thousand attendees, predominantly young adults and their families, reflecting the continued relevance of traditional matchmaking customs in contemporary Indian society. The temple’s management plans to continue the ritual, emphasizing its role in community cohesion and cultural heritage.
author: Al Jazeera

title: 2026 Emmys: Widow’s Bay and The Pitt lead winners as Jean Smart earns fifth award
content:
Jean Smart secured her fifth Primetime Emmy Award on Sunday, winning Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series for the third season of HBO Max’s “Hacks.” The victory marks the first time an actress has been honored with the lead‑comedy award for each season of a single series, underscoring Smart’s consistent critical acclaim throughout the show’s run.

“Hacks,” which follows the unlikely partnership between veteran comedian Deborah Vance (Smart) and her young writer Ava (Hannah Einbinder), has been lauded for its sharp writing and strong performances. Smart’s latest win adds to her previous Emmy honors for the series in 2021 and 2022, while the show itself has accumulated multiple nominations across acting, writing, and directing categories. The achievement highlights both Smart’s enduring presence in television comedy and the series’ sustained relevance in a competitive awards landscape.
author: Al Jazeera

title: 300,000 Olive Ridley Turtles Nest on Southern Mexico Beach
content:
More than 300,000 olive ridley turtles (Lepidochelys olivacea) have gathered on a southern‑Mexico beach for a mass nesting event, known locally as an “arribada.” The unprecedented aggregation was reported this week along the Pacific shoreline of Oaxaca, where the turtles come ashore to lay thousands of eggs each year. Researchers and conservation volunteers counted the animals as they moved in large groups across the sand, noting that the numbers exceed previous records for the site.

The massive turnout underscores the species’ continued reliance on this coastal habitat despite ongoing threats such as illegal egg harvesting, coastal development, and climate‑related changes to nesting conditions. Local authorities have deployed additional patrols and monitoring equipment to protect the nests and gather data that will inform future management strategies. The event provides a critical opportunity to reinforce protection measures and raise public awareness about the importance of preserving olive ridley nesting grounds.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Internet shutdown exceeds 100 days in Pakistan-administered Kashmir
content:
Mobile data and broadband services have been suspended across the territory since June, when large‑scale protests erupted demanding reforms to the electoral system. Authorities imposed the shutdown as part of a broader security response, citing concerns that the internet could be used to coordinate demonstrations and spread disinformation. The suspension affects both residential users and commercial enterprises, disrupting communication, online commerce, and access to information.

Government officials said the measures are temporary and will be lifted once stability is restored, while protest organizers condemned the restrictions as an infringement on freedom of expression and an impediment to their campaign for a more representative voting framework. International observers have called for a transparent review of the shutdown, urging the authorities to balance security considerations with the public’s right to connectivity. The situation remains fluid, with the continuation of the service suspension dependent on developments in the political dialogue and public order.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Leeds United beat Newcastle 4-1 to move to third in Premier League
content:
Leeds United secured a vital three‑point victory in their latest league fixture, with all three goals coming from in‑form forward James Calvert‑Lewin, rising talent Okafor and seasoned striker Bogle. The 3‑1 win over rivals Sheffield Wednesday not only showcased Leeds’ attacking depth but also propelled the club up the standings, moving them from seventh to fifth place with 48 points after 23 matches. Calvert‑Lewin opened the scoring in the 12th minute, capitalising on a well‑executed cross, while Okafor doubled the lead before halftime with a close‑range finish. Bogle sealed the win in the second half, converting a penalty after a defensive error by the opposition.

The result strengthens Leeds’ push for a top‑four finish as the season approaches its decisive phase. Manager [Name] praised the collective effort, emphasizing the importance of maintaining consistency and defensive solidity in upcoming fixtures. With the team now only three points behind the automatic promotion spots, the next few games will be crucial in determining whether Leeds can sustain their momentum and secure a place in the promotion playoffs.
author: Al Jazeera

title: Beef becomes scarce in West Bengal after BJP forms state government
content:
Since the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) assumed control of West Bengal’s state government under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the availability of beef in the region’s eateries has markedly declined. Government officials have cited stricter enforcement of existing cattle protection statutes and the introduction of new licensing requirements for meat vendors as primary factors behind the reduced supply. Traders report that transport routes for cattle have become more constrained, and several wholesale markets have faced temporary shutdowns pending compliance checks, leading to a noticeable drop in the volume of beef reaching local restaurants.
